In this post I use Python to explore how body size differs across three
species of penguins living near Palmer Station, Antarctica.

Data: [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/),
collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
Released under the CC0 licence.

## Setup

```{python}
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
```

## Load and clean the data

```{python}
penguins = load_penguins()
print(penguins.shape)
penguins = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm", "sex"])
print(penguins.shape)
penguins["species"].value_counts().sort_index()
```

I drop the few penguins with missing body mass, flipper length, or sex.

## Body mass by species

```{python}
penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].agg(["count", "mean", "std"]).round(1)
```

## Body mass by species and sex

```{python}
penguins.groupby(["species", "sex"])["body_mass_g"].mean().round(1).unstack()
```

## Flipper length and body mass

```{python}
round(penguins["flipper_length_mm"].corr(penguins["body_mass_g"]), 2)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-penguins-py
#| fig-cap: "Flipper length versus body mass for three penguin species."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for (name, group), color in zip(penguins.groupby("species"), ["#8FA3B5", "#D8A7A7", "#9C88B0"]):
    ax.scatter(group["flipper_length_mm"], group["body_mass_g"], label=name, alpha=0.8, color=color)
ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()
```

## What I found

After removing penguins with missing values, the data contain 333 penguins:
146 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap, and 119 Gentoo. Gentoo penguins are clearly the
largest species, with an average body mass of about 5,092 g. Adelie and
Chinstrap penguins are much lighter and almost identical in size, averaging
about 3,706 g and 3,733 g respectively. Within every species, males are
heavier than females. The gap is largest for Gentoo penguins (about 805 g),
followed by Adelie (about 675 g) and Chinstrap penguins (about 412 g).

Flipper length and body mass are strongly and positively correlated, with a
correlation of 0.87: penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier. In the
scatter plot, Gentoo penguins form their own group in the upper right, with
flipper lengths of roughly 205 to 230 mm. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins
overlap heavily in the lower left, with most flippers between about 180 and
205 mm. The same upward trend also appears within each species, not only
between them.

This means body size alone is enough to pick out a Gentoo penguin, but not to
tell an Adelie from a Chinstrap. The data come from three islands over three
years, so they may not represent all penguins of these species. A natural next
step would be to look at bill length and bill depth, which might help separate
Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.
